The "Substantial Basis in Law" Threshold and Discovery Stay 
Once the defendants demonstrate that the lawsuit targets protected petitioning conduct, 
CPLR 3211(g)(1) triggers a specialized, highly aggressive burden-shifting regime.1 The statute 
mandates that the court "shall" dismiss the complaint unless the plaintiff (Bleich) can 
demonstrate that the cause of action has a "substantial basis in law".1 
Appellate jurisprudence, specifically the First Department’s ruling in Reeves v Associated 
Newspapers, Ltd., clarifies that this is a "proof-sensitive inquiry" that is far more exacting than 
an ordinary motion to dismiss under CPLR 3211(a)(7).1 The court must look beyond mere 
pleadings to determine if the claim is supported by substantial evidence.1 Bleich cannot meet 
this burden because his core factual assertions—such as claiming Article III § 8 of the By-Laws 
restricts Unit 2's occupancy, or claiming FAR ownership of the roof—are demonstrably 
contradicted by the documentary evidence.1 Under Reeves, where documentary evidence 
disproves a core factual assertion, the claim inherently fails the substantial-basis test.1 
Furthermore, filing the CPLR 3211(g) motion triggers an automatic, statutory stay of "all 
discovery, pending hearings, and motions".1 This critical procedural mechanism immediately 
halts Bleich and Giacovas's ability to use the discovery process to artificially inflate Damerau's 
defense costs—neutralizing the exact tactical abuse Giacovas successfully deployed in the 
Medifast litigation.1 
Mandatory Fee Shifting Under Civil Rights Law § 70-a 
The ultimate consequence of Bleich's failed litigation strategy is strict financial liability. Civil 
Rights Law § 70-a(1)(a) provides that in an action involving public petition and participation, 
"costs and attorney’s fees shall be recovered" upon a showing that the action lacked a 
substantial basis in fact and law.1 
Appellate courts, as demonstrated in Reeves and VIP Pet Grooming Studio, Inc. v Sproule, 
interpret the word "shall" as a textual mandate: fee-shifting is mandatory for qualifying cases 
where the plaintiff fails to meet the CPLR 3211(g) burden.1 Because Bleich commenced and 
continued this action based on false premises, misquoted governing documents, and the 
deliberate concealment of his own illegal cellar occupancy to penalize code-compliance 
enforcement, Damerau is statutorily entitled to recover all defense costs.1 While the defense 
may also seek punitive damages under § 70-a(1)(c), this requires a higher evidentiary showing 
that the action was commenced for the "sole purpose" of malicious harassment.1 Nonetheless, 
the mandatory recovery of standard attorneys' fees serves to directly reverse the economic
